title: Postman
summary: Covers HTTP response status codes and their five families, then shows the Express methods for POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE using res.sendStatus. Introduces Postman for testing non-GET routes without building a front end, with an exercise that exercises all five verbs against a provided server.

concepts.heading: Request and response flow
points: The client (desktop, laptop or phone) sends a request to the server side, which includes the machine, the application (index.js) and any database. The server sends a response back.
A response can carry text or HTML, but it can also be just a status code.

concepts.heading: HTTP status code families
points: Codes are three-digit numbers, grouped by first digit (MDN documents them at developer.mozilla.org under Web/HTTP/Status).
100s: informational. 200s: success. 300s: redirection. 400s: client error. 500s: server error.
A memory aid: 1xx means wait or here is some info, 2xx means success, 3xx means go elsewhere, 4xx means the client made a mistake, 5xx means the server has a fault (bug, missing resource).

201 Created: a new resource was created, typical reply to a POST. (Extra) A 201 response may still carry a body or a Location header pointing at the new resource; in this lesson it is sent with no content.
201 Created: a new resource was created, typical after a POST (or PUT) where nothing needs to be sent back.

301: the resource moved permanently and the response gives the new URL. A mistyped domain that redirects to the right site shows this in the browser dev tools Network tab (tick Preserve log, filter All).
404: the server cannot find the requested resource, usually a wrong URL.
(Extra) 200 OK is the general-purpose success code; 201 is specific to creation, so do not treat it as the default success reply.

concepts.heading: Other HTTP methods in Express
points: Express has one method per verb: app.get, app.post, app.put, app.patch and app.delete. Each takes a path and a (req, res) callback, just like app.get.
POST requests usually originate from an HTML form (sign-up page) carrying data in the request body. The server may validate or store it, then replies with 200 plus data or 201 with nothing.
res.sendStatus(code) replies with just a status code (and its standard text) instead of a body. Use it when the route has no content to return.

(Extra) res.sendStatus(code) sets the status and sends the code's standard reason phrase as a plain-text body (201 gives 'Created', 200 gives 'OK'). It is shorthand for res.status(code).send(text). To send a custom body with a status, chain res.status(201).send(...) or res.status(201).json(...).
In a browser address bar only GET routes can be tested, since typing a URL always makes a GET request. The other verbs need a form or a testing tool.

(Extra) Express does not parse a request body by default: inside these handlers req.body is undefined until a body-parsing middleware such as express.urlencoded({ extended: true }) is added (covered in the middleware lessons). Body fields sent from Postman are therefore ignored here.

concepts.heading: Postman
points: Postman is a free desktop API client (postman.com/downloads) for sending HTTP requests to a server without writing a front end. Developers use it to test routes before the front end exists.

Each request tab has a method dropdown (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE), a URL field for the host, port and endpoint, and a Body tab for sending data, such as x-www-form-urlencoded key and value pairs like name and email.
Click Send to fire the request. The response status code, time, size and body appear below; hovering over the status explains its meaning.
Connection refused means nothing is listening on that port, i.e. the server is not running.
PUT is meant to replace a whole resource, so the client would normally send the complete data. PATCH sends only the field(s) to change. DELETE needs just the right path.
Real handlers would update or delete data; in this lesson the routes only return status codes to demonstrate the mechanics.

concepts.heading: Running a downloaded Node project
points: Downloaded projects normally omit node_modules because it is large. cd into the project folder and run npm install with no package names; it reads package.json and installs every listed dependency.
Then start the server with nodemon index.js.

task.name: 3.3 Postman: test all five verbs
task.starting_point: Download and extract the 3.3 Postman zip. It holds an Express server with a GET route at the root, POST /register, and PUT, PATCH and DELETE routes on a user path, all returning status codes. Postman installed.
task.goal: Create one Postman tab per HTTP method and confirm each returns the expected success status code.
steps: cd into the extracted project and run npm install to fetch dependencies.
Start the server with nodemon index.js.
In Postman create a GET request to localhost:3000 (the trailing slash is optional) and Send. Expect the h1 body and status 200.
Create a POST to localhost:3000/register; optionally add urlencoded body fields. Expect 201 Created.
Create a PUT to localhost:3000/user/angela (the path must match the one in index.js exactly). Expect 200 OK.
Create a PATCH to the same user path, optionally with one changed field in the body. Expect 200.
Create a DELETE to the same path. Expect 200.
(Extra) Try a wrong path or method (for example a POST to /user/angela/x) to see Express's 404 'Cannot POST ...' response.
task.expected_result:
Five Postman tabs, each returning the correct status (200, 201, 200, 200, 200), with bodies '

Hello World

', 'Created', 'OK', 'OK', 'OK'. With the server stopped, Postman shows connection refused.

pitfalls: Testing POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE by typing a URL in the browser; that always sends GET and gives Cannot GET or the wrong route.
Using a path in Postman that does not match the one in the server code (the username segment must match), giving 404.
Forgetting npm install after downloading a project, so express is missing.
Connection refused because the server is not running or the port differs.

Reference repo note: the repo uses the student's own username in the user path (replaced with angela in these notes), changes the home h1 text, and adds an extra GET /about route and a status-codes image; the five verb routes otherwise match the lesson.

gaps_and_ideas: Proposed lesson 'Status codes and Postman': blurb on reading response codes and testing verbs.

Tasks: (1) classify codes 200, 201, 301, 404, 500 into their families; (2) pick the right code for a given scenario; (3) read an Express route list and say what each returns; (4) write a PATCH route that returns 200; (5) list the Postman settings for a POST with form data.
Starter code idea: an Express file with app.post and app.put stubs missing their sendStatus calls.
Interactive demo idea: a mini Postman simulator in the page where choosing method and path against a fake route table shows status code, meaning and body, with 404 for unknown routes.
